Altitude Mirror

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: A triangle and the straight line dropped from its top corner hide a mirror trick; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the four dots to move the triangle and the dot on the straight line. Tick the boxes to show the names, the angle marks or the helper lines.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step).

Look for the math

Drop a line straight down from the top corner of a triangle and put a dot anywhere on it. Join that dot to the other two corners. Something unexpected happens at the foot of the line.

The mirror at the foot

Let the straight line from A meet BC at H, and let P be any point on it. The line CP meets AB at E, and BP meets AC at D. When H lies between B and C, the two angles at H are equal: ∠BHE = ∠CHD. The line AH also splits the angle DHE into two equal parts, so it acts like a mirror. The logic test checked this on 648 exact triangles and 4,000 random ones, and it held every time.

Why the two sides are equal

Draw a line through A parallel to BC (the "hint" box shows it). It meets HE at F and HD at G. Similar triangles give AF = AE · BH / BE and AG = AD · CH / CD. Ceva's theorem says (AE/BE) · (BH/CH) · (CD/AD) = 1 when the three cevians meet at P. Multiply it out and the two lengths become the same: AF = AG. That symmetry is the whole proof, due to Hiroshi Haruki. The test checked all three formulas numerically as well.

The orthic triangle

Drag P onto the crossing point of the three altitudes — the orthocenter. Then D and E become the feet of the other two altitudes, and DEH is the orthic triangle. Its sides are equally inclined to the sides of the original triangle; this is the mirror property that solves Fagnano's problem.

When the foot falls outside

The page states the angle equality only when H is between B and C. Make the triangle obtuse at B or C and the foot leaves the side: the two rays HE and HD can then point in opposite directions, so the ordinary angle equality fails in many cases. The underlying mirror of the two lines still holds, and so does AF = AG; the test checked 4,000 such triangles and found no exception.

Try putting P exactly at the orthocenter, then tick "Show statement" and drag A slowly: the two green angle marks stay equal.
